source: Marqu - The Hebrew Gospel of Mark v1.2

verses.translation: And another time{H6471} he entered{H935} Kfar Nachum after some days{H3117}.

And when they knew{H3045} that he was{H1961} in the house{H1004}, a great{H7227} people{H5971} assembled{H622}, and it could not contain{H3557} them, for the whole{H3605} house{H1004} was full{H4392} up to the door{H6607}.

greek_deviations: Greek adds καὶ ἐλάλει αὐτοῖς τὸν λόγον ('and he was speaking the word to them'). Hebrew omits this — the Hebrew narrative is more spare.

verses.translation: And four{H702} men{H376} came{H935} to him, carrying{H5375} one{H259} man{H120} paralyzed, on a bed{H4296}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נטול (natul — 'taken/paralyzed') — a later Hebrew form from the root נטל ('to take/carry'), meaning one whose limbs have been 'taken' from him. Greek παραλυτικόν ('paralytic') is a medical term. The Hebrew is an organic Semitic formation; a back-translator from Greek would use the loanword פראליטיקוס or a biblical term like נכה ('stricken').
translation_notes: 'Paralyzed' for natul — literally 'taken,' meaning his limbs were taken from his control.

verses.translation: And when they could not make a path before him{H6440}, they went up{H5927} on the house{H1004} and broke through it, and brought him up{H5927} on the bed{H4296} and brought him before{H6440} Yeshua{H3442}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses החריבוהו (hecherivuhu — 'they destroyed/broke through it', H2717, from חרב — 'to be desolate/destroy') — a strong verb implying structural demolition. Greek ἀπεστέγασαν ('they unroofed') merely describes removing the roof. The Hebrew implies a more violent breaking; the Greek a more controlled removal. A back-translator from Greek would use פתחו ('opened') or גלו ('uncovered'), not the destruction verb חרב.
greek_deviations: Greek adds ἐξορύξαντες ('having dug through') specifying the method. Hebrew says only 'broke through it' without specifying digging.

verses.translation: And when Yeshua{H3442} saw{H7200} their faith{H530}, he said{H559} to the paralyzed man: Your iniquities{H5771} are pardoned{H4229} to you.

one_way_hebrew: Uses עונות (avonot — 'iniquities', H5771) consistently, not חטאים (chata'im — 'sins'). Greek ἁμαρτίαι ('sins') is generic. The Hebrew maintains the distinction: avon implies guilt and its consequences — a deeper concept than mere 'sin.'
Uses מחולין (mochalin — 'pardoned', from H4229 מחל — 'to pardon/wipe') — a later Hebrew form meaning full pardon. Greek ἀφέωνται ('are forgiven/released'). The Hebrew implies a complete wiping clean.

verses.translation: And there were{H1961} with him some of the wise-ones of the law, and they thought{H2803} in their heart{H3820}, saying{H559}:
words: of the wise-ones of the law

one_way_hebrew: Again uses חכמי הדת ('wise-ones of the law') for scribes — consistent with Mark 1:22. This respectful Hebrew designation contrasts with the Greek functional term γραμματεῖς ('scribes/copyists').

verses.translation: How does he speak{H1696} thus? This is a curse{H7045}! For who can atone{H3722} for iniquities{H5771} except God{H410} alone?

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses קללה (qelalah — 'curse', H7045) for the scribes' accusation. Greek βλασφημίας ('blasphemy') is a Greek religious concept. The Hebrew uses the Torah word for curse (Gen 27:12-13, Deut 11:26-28, 21:23, 27:13). The accusation in Hebrew is that he has pronounced a curse (by usurping God's prerogative), not 'blasphemy' in the Greek sense. A back-translator from Greek would use a transliteration or גידוף (giduf — 'reviling'), not the Torah concept of curse.

CRITICAL: Uses לכפר (lechaper — 'to atone for', H3722) — again the Yom Kippur verb. Greek ἀφιέναι ('to forgive/release') is simply 'to let go.' The wise-ones frame the issue in atonement terms: who can perform the priestly act of kapparah? A back-translator from Greek would use למחול ('to forgive'), not לכפר ('to atone').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'curse' (קללה — Torah concept). Greek: 'blasphemy' (βλασφημία — Greek religious concept).
Hebrew: 'atone for iniquities' (כפר — priestly act). Greek: 'forgive sins' (ἀφιέναι — legal release).
translation_notes: 'Curse' for qelalah preserves the Torah legal framework — the scribes see a Torah violation, not a Greek-style blasphemy.

verses.translation: And immediately he perceived{H5234} their thoughts{H4284} through the Holy{H6918} Spirit{H7307}, and said{H559} to them: What do you think{H2803} in your hearts{H3824}?

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew explicitly attributes the perception to the Holy Spirit (בעד הקדוש רוח — 'through the Holy Spirit'). Greek says only τῷ πνεύματι αὐτοῦ ('in his spirit' — lowercase, his own spirit). The Hebrew elevates this to the divine Holy Spirit; the Greek attributes it to Yeshua's own perception. A back-translator from Greek would write ברוחו ('in his spirit'), not 'through the Holy Spirit.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'through the Holy Spirit.' Greek: 'in his own spirit.' Different source of knowledge.

verses.translation: Which is the easier{H7043} word{H4405} — to say{H559} to the paralyzed: 'Your iniquities{H5771} are pardoned,' or to say{H559}: 'Rise{H6965}, take{H3947} your bed{H4296} and carry it to your house{H1004} and go{H1980}'?

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'carry it to your house and go' (expanded). Greek: 'take up your bed and walk' (simpler). Hebrew adds the destination.
translation_notes: מלה (milah, H4405 — 'word/utterance') — the poetic/wisdom word for speech (Job 4:2, 6:26; Ps 19:5), distinct from דבר (davar — 'word/matter').

verses.translation: But so that you may know{H3045} that the Son of the Virgin{H1330} has power to release{H5800} the iniquities{H5771} on the earth{H776}, he said{H559} to the paralyzed:

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses בן הבתולה ('Son of the Virgin', H1121+H1330) where Greek has ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ('the Son of Man'). This is a completely different christological title. בתולה (betulah — 'virgin') is the Hebrew word for a young woman who has not known a man (Gen 24:16, Isa 7:14 LXX). No back-translator from Greek 'Son of Man' would produce 'Son of the Virgin.' This title connects directly to the virgin birth tradition (Isa 7:14) and is absent from all Greek Gospel manuscripts.

Uses לעזוב (la'azov — 'to release/abandon', H5800, from עזב) — meaning to let go, to release. Greek ἀφιέναι ('to forgive/release') is semantically close, but the Hebrew עזב carries the sense of abandoning/leaving behind — the iniquities are abandoned, not merely forgiven.
greek_deviations: MAJOR: Hebrew: 'Son of the Virgin' (בן הבתולה). Greek: 'Son of Man' (υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου). Entirely different christological title.
translation_notes: 'Son of the Virgin' — a christological title absent from all Greek manuscripts, connecting to Isaiah 7:14.
textual_notes: Isaiah 7:14: הִנֵּה הָעַלְמָה הָרָה וְיֹלֶדֶת בֵּן — 'Behold, the young woman is pregnant and bearing a son.' The LXX renders עלמה as παρθένος ('virgin'). The Hebrew Gospel uses the explicit בתולה ('virgin') rather than עלמה ('young woman').

verses.translation: Go — I say{H559} to you: Rise{H6965} and take{H3947} your bed{H4296}.

And immediately he rose{H6965} and took{H3947} his bed{H4296} and went{H1980} before all{H3605}, so that all{H3605} were astonished{H8539} and blessed{H1288} God{H410}, saying{H559}: Never have we seen{H7200} such a thing{H1697}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses וברכו את האל ('and they blessed God', H1288 — from ברך 'to bless'). Greek ἐδόξαζον τὸν θεόν ('they glorified God'). The Hebrew response is blessing — the standard Jewish liturgical response to witnessing God's power (the berakhah tradition). The Greek response is glorification. A back-translator from Greek would use כבדו ('glorified'), not ברכו ('blessed').

verses.translation: And he went out{H3318} from there to go again to the sea{H3220}, and all{H3605} the people{H5971} came{H935}, and he was teaching them.

translation_notes: The phrase מראה וילונים is textually difficult. The sense from context and the Greek parallel (ἐδίδασκεν αὐτούς — 'he was teaching them') is that he was instructing the crowd.

verses.translation: And passing{H5674} through a certain place{H4725}, he saw{H7200} Levi at his feet — that is Mattityahu{H4993} — sitting{H3427} at the table{H7979}, and said{H559} to him: Draw{H4900} yourself after me. And he rose{H6965} and drew after him.

one_way_hebrew: Uses תמשך אחרי ('draw yourself after me', H4900 from משך — 'to draw/pull'). Greek ἀκολούθει μοι ('follow me') is a simple command. The Hebrew verb meshekh carries the image of being drawn or pulled — as in Jeremiah 31:3: 'with lovingkindness I have drawn you' (משכתיך). The call is not mere following but being drawn by attraction. A back-translator from Greek would use הלך אחרי ('walk after'), not the magnetic משך.
Identifies Levi as מתתיהו (Mattityahu — 'gift of Yah', H4993). Greek does not make this identification in Mark (only in Matthew's Gospel). The Hebrew adds this cross-reference naturally.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'sitting at the table' (בשלחן — 'at the table'). Greek: καθήμενον ἐπὶ τὸ τελώνιον ('sitting at the tax office'). Completely different setting — a dining table vs. a tax booth.
Hebrew identifies Levi as Mattityahu. Greek Mark does not.
translation_notes: 'Draw' for timshekh preserves the magnetic-attraction metaphor of the Hebrew verb.

verses.translation: And it came to pass{H6213} while they were eating{H398} in the house{H1004}, many{H7227} debauchees and sinners{H2400} eating{H398} with Yeshua{H3442} and his students{H8527}, and there were many{H7227} there who walked{H1980} after him.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses עוגבים (ogvim — 'debauchees/lustful ones', from עגב — 'to lust/desire excessively'). Greek τελωνῶν ('tax collectors'). These are entirely different categories — moral debauchees vs. economic functionaries. No back-translator from Greek 'tax collectors' would produce 'debauchees.' The Hebrew categorizes these people by moral character; the Greek by profession.

Uses תלמידים (talmidim — 'students', H8527) — the native Hebrew term for disciples, from the root למד ('to learn'). Greek μαθηταί ('learners/disciples') is a semantic equivalent but the Hebrew word carries the full Torah-study tradition of the master-student relationship.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'debauchees and sinners' (עוגבים וחטאים). Greek: 'tax collectors and sinners' (τελωνῶν καὶ ἁμαρτωλῶν). Different first category.
translation_notes: 'Debauchees' for ogvim — from the root עגב meaning excessive desire/lust.

verses.translation: And when the letter-workers and the Perushim{H6567} saw{H7200} that Yeshua{H3442} eats{H398} with the debauchees and with the sinners{H2400}, they said{H559} to his students{H8527}: Why does your rabbi eat{H398} and drink{H8354} with the debauchees and the sinners{H2400}?

one_way_hebrew: Uses המאותתים (ha-me'otetim — 'the letter-workers') — apparently from אות/אותיות ('letter/sign'), describing scribes by their occupation with letters. Greek γραμματεῖς ('scribes') is from γράμμα ('letter') — a parallel concept but independently formed. The Hebrew creates its own occupational title from אות rather than borrowing the Greek term.
Uses רבנכם (rabbankhem — 'your rabbi/master') — a term of respect absent from Greek, which has only the pronoun 'he.' The Hebrew preserves the social dynamic of respectful address to a teacher.
Uses פרושים (Perushim, from H6567 פרש — 'to separate/distinguish') — the native Hebrew name meaning 'the separated ones.' Greek Φαρισαῖοι is a transliteration of this Hebrew word.
greek_deviations: Hebrew adds 'your rabbi' (רבנכם) — absent from Greek, which says simply 'he.'
translation_notes: 'Perushim' preserved untranslated — meaning 'the separated ones,' those who separate themselves for ritual purity.

verses.translation: And Yeshua{H3442} heard{H8085} this and said{H559}: The healthy{H1293} have no need of a healer{H7495}, only those who have illness{H2483}. For I have not come{H935} to call{H7121} the righteous{H6662} but the sinners{H2400}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses רופא (rofeh — 'healer', H7495) — the OT word for a physician/healer (Gen 50:2, Ex 15:26 — 'I am YHWH your healer', 2 Chr 16:12, Jer 8:22). Greek ἰατρός ('physician') is the medical professional. The Hebrew carries the resonance of YHWH as Israel's healer.
greek_deviations: Greek adds εἰς μετάνοιαν ('to repentance') at the end. Hebrew has only 'to call the sinners' without specifying the purpose.

verses.translation: And the students{H8527} of Yochanan{H3110} and some of the Perushim{H6567} were fasting{H6684}, and they said{H559} to Yeshua{H3442}: Why do the students{H8527} of Yochanan{H3110} and the Perushim{H6567} fast{H6684}, but your students{H8527} do not fast{H6684}?
And Yeshua{H3442} said{H559} to them: Those who are near to a wedding{H5375} — how can they fast{H6684} while the bridegroom{H2860} is with them?

one_way_hebrew: Uses נישואין (nisuin — 'wedding/marriage', from H5375 נשא — 'to lift/carry') — the standard Hebrew legal term for the marriage ceremony. Greek νηστεύειν ('to fast') context has υἱοὶ τοῦ νυμφῶνος ('sons of the bridal chamber') — a Semitic idiom preserved in Greek. The Hebrew uses the native legal term for marriage rather than the Semitic idiom.

Uses קרובים לנישואין ('near to a wedding') — describing the wedding party. Greek 'sons of the bridal chamber' is a Hebrew idiom that the Greek preserves. The Hebrew text uses a different, more natural expression.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'those near to a wedding.' Greek: 'sons of the bridal chamber' (υἱοὶ τοῦ νυμφῶνος — a Semiticism). Different idiom for the same concept.

verses.translation: But the time{H6256} approaches when the bridegroom{H2860} shall be seized{H1497} from you, and in that time{H6256} they shall fast{H6684} many{H7227} days{H3117}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses יגזל (yigazel — 'shall be seized/robbed', H1497 from גזל — 'to rob/seize by force'). Greek ἀπαρθῇ ('shall be taken away') is a gentle removal. The Hebrew verb implies violent seizure — robbery (Gen 21:25, Lev 19:13, Deut 28:29, Mic 2:2). The bridegroom is not merely 'taken away' but forcibly seized. A back-translator from Greek would use ילקח ('shall be taken'), not the violent גזל. This foreshadows the violent arrest and crucifixion.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'seized' (גזל — violent robbery). Greek: 'taken away' (ἀπαίρω — gentle removal). Different characterization of the event.
translation_notes: 'Seized' for yigazel preserves the violence of the Hebrew verb — the bridegroom is robbed from them, not merely removed.

verses.translation: No man{H120} puts a new{H2319} cloth{H899} on his old{H3465} garment{H4403}; otherwise the new{H2319} cloth{H899} tears{H7665} the old{H3465}, and a greater{H1419} rend is made{H6213}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שובר (shover — 'breaks/tears', H7665) — the verb for breaking pottery, breaking bones, breaking covenants (Jer 19:10-11, Ex 12:46, Isa 24:5). Greek αἴρει ('takes away/tears off') is simpler removal. The Hebrew implies destructive breaking — the new tears the old apart.

verses.translation: And no man{H120} puts new{H2319} wine{H3196} in old{H3465} wineskins, for the old{H3465} wineskins burst and the wine{H3196} spills. But one must put new{H2319} wine{H3196} in new{H2319} wineskins.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נאדות (ne'odot — 'wineskins', H4997) — the OT word for leather water/wine containers (Josh 9:4,13; Judg 4:19; 1 Sam 16:20; Ps 119:83). Greek ἀσκούς ('skins') is the direct equivalent. The Hebrew maintains the biblical vocabulary.

verses.translation: And it came to pass{H6213} another time{H6471} that he was passing{H5674} through places of grain{H2233} on the Shabbat{H7676}, and his students{H8527} began to break off{H7665} from the stalks.

one_way_hebrew: Uses קוצים (qotsim — 'thorns/stalks', H6975) — the word typically meaning 'thorns' but here referring to grain stalks or ears. Greek στάχυας ('heads of grain') is specific. The Hebrew word choice is unusual — either a dialectal usage or the author sees the grain differently than the Greek tradition.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'break off from the stalks' (לשבור מהקוצים). Greek: τίλλειν τοὺς στάχυας ('to pluck the heads of grain'). Different action — breaking vs. plucking.

verses.translation: And the Perushim{H6567} said{H559} to him: Your students{H8527} do{H6213} on the Shabbat{H7676} what is not proper to do{H6213}.
And Yeshua{H3442} said{H559} to them: Have you not read{H7121} what David{H1732} did{H6213}, he and his soldiers{H2428}, when they were hungry{H7456}?

one_way_hebrew: Uses חיילותיו (chaylotav — 'his soldiers/troops', H2428, from חיל) — specifically identifying David's companions as military personnel. Greek μετ' αὐτοῦ ('with those with him') is vague. The Hebrew reflects knowledge of the 1 Samuel 21 narrative where David's companions are indeed armed soldiers on a mission. A back-translator from Greek would write אותם שהיו עמו ('those who were with him'), not the military term.
textual_notes: Reference to 1 Samuel 21:1-6 where David comes to Nob and receives the showbread from Ahimelech the priest.

verses.translation: That he entered{H935} the sanctuary{H4720} under Evyatar{H54} the chief{H8269} of the priests{H3548}, and ate{H398} the bread{H3899} of holiness{H6944} — which no man{H120} is worthy to eat{H398} except the priests{H3548} — he ate{H398} and gave{H5414} to his soldiers{H2428}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מקדש (miqdash — 'sanctuary', H4720) — the standard Hebrew term for the sacred precinct. Greek εἰς τὸν οἶκον τοῦ θεοῦ ('into the house of God'). The Hebrew uses the specific OT sanctuary term (Ex 25:8, Lev 12:4); the Greek uses a general 'house of God.'

Uses שר הכהנים ('chief of the priests', H8269+H3548) — using שר (sar — 'prince/commander') rather than כהן גדול ('great priest' / high priest). Greek ἀρχιερέως ('high priest'). The Hebrew title implies a military-administrative commander of the priestly corps. A back-translator from Greek would write כהן גדול.

Uses לחמי הקדש ('bread of holiness', H3899+H6944) — echoing 1 Samuel 21:5-7. Greek τοὺς ἄρτους τῆς προθέσεως ('the bread of the setting-forth/showbread'). The Hebrew preserves the 1 Samuel terminology; the Greek uses the Pentateuchal technical term.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the sanctuary' (מקדש). Greek: 'the house of God.' Different designation.
Hebrew: 'chief of the priests' (שר). Greek: 'high priest' (ἀρχιερεύς). Different title.
textual_notes: Historical note: 1 Samuel 21 names the priest as Ahimelech, not Abiathar (Evyatar). Both the Hebrew and Greek Mark name Abiathar — a shared tradition, possibly because Abiathar was Ahimelech's son who survived the Nob massacre (1 Sam 22:20) and became the more famous high priest.

verses.translation: And he said{H559}: The Shabbat{H7676} was made{H6213} for{H5668} the man{H120}, and the man{H120} was not for{H5668} the Shabbat{H7676}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses האדם (ha-adam — 'the man/mankind', H120, with definite article) — echoing Genesis 1-2 where 'the adam' is the archetypal human. The Shabbat was made for 'the adam' — the same being for whom the entire creation was made. Greek τὸν ἄνθρωπον is merely 'man.' The Hebrew connects the saying to the creation narrative.
textual_notes: The Mekhilta on Exodus 31:13 contains a parallel: 'The Shabbat was given to you, not you to the Shabbat.' This Hebrew saying circulated in rabbinic tradition.

verses.translation: And therefore the son{H1121} of God{H433} is master{H113} of all{H3605} that is in the world{H5769}, and of the Shabbat{H7676}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses בן האלוה ('Son of God', H1121+H433) where Greek has ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ('the Son of Man'). As in v.10 (which uses 'Son of the Virgin'), the Hebrew Gospel avoids the title 'Son of Man' entirely, using different christological titles. No back-translator from Greek would replace 'Son of Man' with 'Son of God.'

Uses אדון מכל מה שהוא בעולם ('master of all that is in the world') — an expansive claim far beyond the Greek's κύριος τοῦ σαββάτου ('lord of the Sabbath'). The Hebrew extends mastery to all creation, with the Shabbat as one example.
Again uses אלוה (eloah, H433) — the rare singular form, consistent with 1:1.
greek_deviations: MAJOR: Hebrew: 'Son of God' (בן האלוה). Greek: 'Son of Man' (υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου). Different christological title.
Hebrew: 'master of all that is in the world, and of the Shabbat.' Greek: 'lord of the Sabbath.' The Hebrew is far more expansive.

chapter_notes.summary: Mark 2 in Hebrew contains several striking deviations from the Greek text. The most significant are: (1) 'Son of the Virgin' (בן הבתולה, v.10) and 'Son of God' (בן האלוה, v.28) replacing Greek 'Son of Man' — entirely different christological titles that no back-translator would produce; (2) קללה ('curse', v.7) vs. Greek 'blasphemy' — framing the accusation in Torah legal terms; (3) לכפר ('atone', v.7) vs. Greek 'forgive' — Yom Kippur vocabulary; (4) עוגבים ('debauchees', v.15-16) vs. Greek 'tax collectors' — moral vs. professional categorization; (5) יגזל ('seized/robbed', v.20) vs. Greek 'taken away' — violent seizure of the bridegroom; (6) חיילותיו ('soldiers', v.25-26) — identifying David's companions with military precision; (7) שר הכהנים ('chief of the priests', v.26) vs. 'high priest'; (8) רבנכם ('your rabbi', v.16) absent from Greek. The chapter reveals a Hebrew text with its own theological vocabulary and christological framework independent of the Greek tradition.
